title: Tritan vs PET vs polystyrene: which drinkware material should you specify?
h1: Tritan vs PET vs polystyrene: which drinkware material should you specify?
author: BYF BOOM Product Team
excerpt: The four materials in our catalogue behave differently under dishwashing, sunlight and freight. Here is how to choose between them without over-buying.
seoTitle: Tritan vs PET vs Polystyrene Drinkware: Which Material to Choose
seoDescription: A buyer's guide to Tritan, PET, polystyrene, polypropylene and acrylic drinkware: clarity, wash-cycle tolerance, durability, freight weight and cost per unit, compared.

sections.h2: The short answer
body: Specify Tritan when the glass has to survive a commercial dishwasher and be reused for years — hotel pool bars, resorts, venues with a glass ban. Specify PET when the priority is the lowest possible unit cost and freight weight for an event or a single season. Specify polystyrene (PS) when you need the clearest, most glass-like appearance at volume and you can accept hand washing for longest life. Specify polypropylene (PP) when the item has to tolerate heat and repeated washing but you do not need crystal clarity. Specify acrylic when the buyer's main complaint is that plastic feels cheap, and a heavier, more premium hand feel justifies a higher unit price.

sections.h2: How the materials actually differ
body: Clarity is the first thing a buyer notices and the last thing a specification sheet explains. PS and acrylic give the closest visual match to glass — they are what you see in a hotel lobby bar where guests assume the glassware is real. PET is clear but reads slightly softer, and it is the material most likely to dull over a season of use. Tritan and PP sit in between: both are clear at first, though Tritan holds its clarity far longer under repeated washing, which is precisely why it costs more.

Durability under impact is where Tritan separates from the pack. All the materials in this catalogue are reusable in normal service, but Tritan is the one designed for a pool deck where glasses get knocked off tables onto concrete and then washed nine times a day.

Heat tolerance decides whether a dishwasher is available to you at all. Tritan, PP and AS tolerate commercial wash temperatures on the top rack. PS and acrylic should be hand washed or top-rack rinsed; hot cycles and harsh detergents dull the polished surface. PET should not go into a hot cycle at all.

sections.h2: Freight weight is a real cost line
body: Unit weight is the specification buyers most often ignore, and it shows up in the freight invoice. A stemless PET wine glass at 20 g is roughly 40% lighter than the Tritan equivalent at 32 g. Across a 5,000-piece order that difference changes the container cube and the landed cost per guest, which is why event buyers often choose PET even when they could afford Tritan.

For heavier items — stemmed glasses and ice buckets — the carton count matters as much as the unit weight. A 12 L ice bucket packing five pieces per carton is a very different freight proposition from a 1 L bucket packing 36.

sections.h2: Choosing by application
bullets: Hotel or resort pool bar, dishwashed daily: Tritan
Wedding or event caterer, packed and re-used across bookings: Tritan for stemware, PET for high-volume stemless
Single-event service where pack-down speed matters more than longevity: PET
Lobby bar or restaurant where the glass must read as crystal: PS or acrylic
Beer service at volume with heavy handling: PS with heavier base walls, PP where heat tolerance matters
Retail or gift where the hand feel drives the price point: acrylic
body: A common and sensible split is Tritan for the items that are washed and reused, and PET or PS for the items that are given away or replaced each season. Mixing materials inside one silhouette family is fine — the shapes match, and the buyer only sees the profile, not the polymer code.

sections.h2: What to put in the specification
body: When you write a specification for a drinkware order, state the material, the capacity, the unit weight, the washing guidance and the carton count. Those five data points determine the guest experience, the replacement cycle and the freight cost. Every product in our catalogue lists all five, which means you can build a specification without asking for a sample first.

faqs.q: Can Tritan drinkware be washed commercially?
faqs.a: Yes. Tritan is intended for the top rack of a commercial dishwasher and is designed to hold its clarity across repeated commercial cycles, which is the main reason it costs more than polystyrene.

faqs.q: Is PET drinkware reusable?
faqs.a: Yes, PET drinkware is reusable, but it is intended for a limited number of cycles. It should be hand washed and is not suited to hot wash cycles.

faqs.q: Which material looks most like real glass?
faqs.a: Polystyrene and acrylic give the closest visual match to glass. Acrylic additionally has a heavier hand feel, which is why it reads as premium in a hotel or restaurant setting.

faqs.q: What material documentation is issued with an order?
faqs.a: Each SKU records its polymer type and grade on the specification table, and that table is the record the quotation is issued against. Safety data sheets and any food-contact test report for the exact grade supplied are issued with the quotation. We do not publish an additive-by-additive statement unless a report for that exact grade is on file — if your destination market needs a specific declaration, tell us which one and we will confirm what we can issue.

faqs.q: Which material should be chosen for repeated commercial washing?
faqs.a: Tritan and polypropylene are the materials intended for repeated washing, and AS holds clarity in larger bowls. PET and polystyrene are the lower-cost routes and are better suited to shorter service life or hand washing.

faqs.q: Does the material change the MOQ?
faqs.a: Yes, potentially. MOQ follows the SKU and the mould, and the material affects the production route, so the confirmed minimum is issued for the exact SKU and material you select.

faqs.q: Can a mixed-material order be consolidated?
faqs.a: Yes. Mixed-material orders are consolidated into a single shipment and a single customs entry, with the material stated per SKU for classification.

title: How many glasses do you need per guest at a wedding or event?
h1: How many glasses do you need per guest at a wedding or event?
author: BYF BOOM Events Team
excerpt: A working formula for glassware quantities by service style, plus the breakage allowance that stops you running short on the night.
seoTitle: How Many Glasses Per Guest at a Wedding? Planning Formula
seoDescription: Work out glassware quantities for weddings and events: glasses per guest by service style, the split between flutes and wine glasses, and the breakage allowance to add.
keywords: how many glasses per guest wedding

sections.h2: The working numbers
body: For a full-service reception with a champagne toast, a cocktail hour and wine with dinner, plan on 2.5 glasses per guest. Split that roughly half champagne flutes for the toast and half all-purpose wine glasses for the rest of the evening. Add a 10% allowance for breakage and loss if the bar is outdoors or if the venue's staff are handling the glassware.
A 200-guest reception therefore needs about 500 pieces: roughly 250 flutes and 250 wine glasses, plus 50 spare. That lands on a comfortable carton count for most of our moulded shapes.

sections.h2: Adjusting by service style
bullets: Champagne toast only, drinks in the venue's own glassware: 1.2 pieces per guest
Cocktail hour plus wine with dinner: 2.0 pieces per guest
Full reception with toast, cocktail hour and wine service: 2.5 pieces per guest
Open bar with a cocktail programme: 3.0 pieces per guest, weighted towards stemless and coupe shapes
Beach, pool or garden setting: add 15% rather than 10% for loss
body: If the venue runs its own bar glassware and you are only supplying the toast, the quantity drops dramatically — this is the single most common reason a first-time buyer over-orders. Ask the venue what they are already providing before you place the order.

sections.h2: Why the split between shapes matters
body: It is tempting to buy all champagne flutes because the toast is the photograph you care about. In practice, flutes are poor all-purpose glasses: they hold too little for a wine pour and guests will return to the bar more often. A 50/50 split between flutes and a general wine glass keeps the toast looking right and keeps the rest of the evening working.
If the bar is serving cocktails, swap part of the wine glass allocation for a coupe or a lowball. A ribbed coupe photographs as well as a flute and works for both a cocktail hour and a dessert wine.

sections.h2: Do not forget the rest of the table
bullets: One ice bucket per two tables for a chilled service
A spittoon or dump bucket if there is a tasting element
Water glasses at roughly one per guest, refilled in place
Spare flutes for a late toast, kept boxed and unwashed
body: Consolidating all of this into one supplier matters more than the unit price. Glassware, buckets and spare stock arriving separately means separate freight, separate delivery windows and a real risk that the spares turn up after the event.

faqs.q: How many glasses do I need for 200 guests?
faqs.a: For a full reception with a champagne toast, cocktail hour and wine service, plan on about 500 pieces — roughly 250 flutes and 250 wine glasses — plus a 10% breakage allowance, so about 550 pieces in total.

faqs.q: Should I buy flutes or wine glasses?
faqs.a: Buy both. A 50/50 split keeps the toast looking right without forcing guests to drink wine from a flute, which pours too small and sends people back to the bar.

faqs.q: How much breakage should I allow for?
faqs.a: Add 10% for an indoor event and 15% for an outdoor, beach or pool setting. Modern moulded drinkware breaks far less than glass, but the allowance covers loss and keeps you from running short.

faqs.q: Can I reuse the glasses for the next event?
faqs.a: Yes, if you specify the right material. Tritan and PP tolerate commercial dishwashing and are designed for repeat use, while PET is the economical choice for single-event service.

faqs.q: How do we convert a guest count into a case quantity?
faqs.a: Convert the guest count into glasses per guest, then into units, then into case packs for the SKUs you selected. Send the guest count, the number of drinks per guest and the SKUs so the case quantity is confirmed against the actual pack size.

faqs.q: Should the keepsake glass be counted separately?
faqs.a: Yes. If the glass leaves with the guest, the keepsake quantity is planned separately from the glasses used during service, because the two are replaced on different cycles.

faqs.q: How should a breakage allowance be planned?
faqs.a: Plan the allowance from the venue, the surface being used and whether the glass is collected during service. Confirm the venue conditions with us and we will state the quantity basis in the quotation.

title: Custom logo drinkware: MOQs, print methods and an artwork checklist
h1: Custom logo drinkware: MOQs, print methods and an artwork checklist
author: BYF BOOM Customisation Team
excerpt: What drives the minimum order on a decorated item, which print method to specify, and exactly what to send us so the proof matches the production run.
seoTitle: Custom Logo Drinkware: MOQs, Print Methods and Artwork Checklist
seoDescription: How minimum order quantities are set for custom logo drinkware, how pad printing compares with laser engraving and electroplating, and the artwork checklist to send.
keywords: pad printing vs laser engraving glassware

sections.h2: What actually sets the minimum order
body: The MOQ on a decorated order is not arbitrary. It is driven by three things: the setup cost of the decoration process, the print position, and the risk of a colour mismatch across a run. Setup is a fixed cost — the screen or pad tooling, the machine time to dial in registration, and the first-off approval. Spread across 200 pieces it is unaffordable; spread across 5,000 it disappears.

In practice the minimum is set by the process and by the print area rather than by a single house number. Multi-colour work and full-wrap artwork rise from there because each colour adds a setup and a registration step. Laser engraving has a higher setup but needs no ink and no drying, which can make it competitive on longer runs.

For small bar tools — pourers, stoppers, sippers — the print area is small enough that minimums can be lower than for drinkware. It is worth asking, because a campaign can be built across two budget lines by quoting the small bar tool and the glassware in the same request.

sections.h2: Choosing between the print methods
bullets: Pad printing — one or two colours, fine detail on curved surfaces, lowest unit cost. The default choice for corporate and event programmes.
Silk screen — larger and flatter print areas, heavier ink coverage, good for a bold single-colour mark.
Laser engraving — the mark is cut into the surface, so it cannot wear off. Choose this where the item will be washed repeatedly or gifted as a keepsake.
Electroplating with a logo — a metallic or mirror finish with the mark integrated into the finish. Used on premium bar tools and novelty drinkware.
Moulded-in logo — the mark is part of the tool itself. The most durable option, and realistic on high-volume shapes where the tooling cost can be amortised.
body: The most common mistake is choosing pad printing for an item that will be washed in a commercial dishwasher for three years. If the buyer's environment is hospitality, laser engraving is usually the right answer even though the unit cost is higher.

sections.h2: The artwork checklist
bullets: Vector format: AI, EPS or PDF. Bitmap files must be redrawn, which adds cost and time.
Pantone reference for every colour, plus a reference for any colour match on the product itself
The exact print position and maximum print dimensions
Text converted to outlines so there is no font substitution
Any trademark or licensed mark, with confirmation that the buyer holds the rights
The channel the product is going into — corporate giveaway, retail shelf, or e-commerce listing
body: The last item on that list changes the packaging answer. A corporate giveaway needs a plain export carton; a retail shelf needs a printed colour box, a hang tag and a UPC barcode. Telling us the channel at quotation stage means packaging is priced into the unit cost instead of appearing as a surprise later.

sections.h2: Approval gates: proof, sample, then production
body: Every decorated programme runs through two gates. First a virtual proof, where you check layout, scale and colour against your artwork. Second, where the finish is colour-sensitive, a physical pre-production sample for sign-off. Nothing enters bulk production until you approve in writing.

This is what stops the classic failure mode of branded orders: a client approving a description of a colour rather than a physical item, then rejecting the shipment because the shade is not what they imagined. A colour chip costs a fraction of a rejected container.

faqs.q: What is the minimum order for logo printing?
faqs.a: The minimum for each decoration method is confirmed per SKU and per decoration method in the quotation.

faqs.q: Is laser engraving better than printing?
faqs.a: Laser engraving is more durable because the mark is cut into the material rather than applied to the surface. Pad printing is cheaper per unit for short runs. For hospitality items that will be washed repeatedly, engraving is usually the right choice.

faqs.q: What file format do you need for artwork?
faqs.a: Vector artwork in AI, EPS or PDF, with text converted to outlines. Send bitmap files if that is all you have and we will confirm whether they can be redrawn and what that costs.

faqs.q: Can you print our logo in a specific Pantone colour?
faqs.a: Yes. Send the Pantone reference and we will produce a colour chip or moulded sample for approval before production starts.

faqs.q: Why does each SKU have its own MOQ?
faqs.a: MOQ is maintained at SKU/model level because it follows the mould, the material and the decoration route for that exact model. It is never calculated from a category name, so two similar-looking items can carry different minimums.

faqs.q: Why do the standard order, the decorated order and the gift-box build have different MOQs?
faqs.a: The blank bulk order, the logo decoration and the custom gift-box build are three different production routes. Each one has its own setup and its own minimum for the same model, so a single figure would be misleading.

faqs.q: Which order inputs determine the final MOQ?
faqs.a: The SKU, the quantity, the decoration method, the decoration area, the packaging configuration and the destination. Change any one of them and the confirmed minimum can change with it.

faqs.q: When should a buyer choose a standard SKU instead of a new packaging configuration?
faqs.a: Choose the standard configuration when the requirement is the item itself. Choose a new packaging configuration when the retail or gift presentation is part of what you are selling, because that route carries its own setup and minimum.

faqs.q: What should a buyer prepare before asking for a custom quote?
faqs.a: The SKU or product link, the quantity, the logo file, the decoration and packaging requirement, the destination country and the target delivery date. With those inputs the MOQ, the production route and the freight basis are all confirmed in one quotation.

faqs.q: How should a distributor plan the first order quantity?
faqs.a: Plan the first quantity from the confirmed MOQ for the exact configuration and the sell-through you expect on that model, then hold the balance of the range for the reorder. Send the model list and the expected volumes so the quantities are quoted together.

title: What US buyers should know about 2026 import duty on plastic drinkware
h1: What US buyers should know about 2026 import duty on plastic drinkware
author: BYF BOOM Export Team
excerpt: Duty on plastic tableware is not one number. It is a base rate plus trade-action layers plus fees, and the classification you choose changes which layers apply.
seoTitle: 2026 US Import Duty on Plastic Drinkware: What Buyers Should Know
seoDescription: How US import duty on plastic drinkware and barware stacks up in 2026, why classification between HTS 3924.10 and 3924.90 changes the total, and how consolidation reduces fees.

sections.h2: Duty is a stack, not a rate
body: When a supplier quotes you "the tariff", they are usually quoting one layer. In reality a US entry can carry four separate charges on the same customs value: the ordinary most-favoured-nation rate from the product's own subheading, a Section 301 trade-action rate from Chapter 99, and then two fees — the merchandise processing fee and, on ocean freight, the harbour maintenance fee.

For plastic household and tableware articles under heading 3924 the ordinary rate is 3.4%. The trade-action layer is what people mean when they say "the China tariff", and crucially it is additive: the schedule reads "the duty provided in the applicable subheading plus 25%", not "25% instead of". You keep the base rate and gain another.

Newer trade actions have added further layers. A separate Section 301 action covering forced labour took effect on 24 July 2026, adding a further charge in Chapter 99. The practical effect is that the effective duty on Chinese-origin plastic tableware is now materially higher than the headline base rate most suppliers quote.

sections.h2: Why classification changes the total
body: Heading 3924 splits between 3924.10, which covers tableware and kitchenware such as cups, plates and cutlery, and 3924.90, the residual break for other household articles. Both carry a 3.4% base rate, but they have been administered under different Section 301 lists, and that difference is what drives the total.

The lesson for buyers is not to shop for a friendlier code — it is to make sure the code is right, and to ask your supplier for the product information your customs broker needs to classify it correctly. Material composition, intended use, whether an item is tableware or a household article, and whether the product incorporates an electrical component all affect the analysis. Get the classification right before you agree a landed cost, not after.

sections.h2: The category that escapes the worst of it
body: This is the most under-used lever in the whole discussion. Items classified as electrical goods rather than plastic tableware — rechargeable wine openers, electric salt and pepper grinders, milk frothers, coffee grinders — sit in a materially different duty position from a polystyrene wine glass. They also carry far higher unit values, which means the same container generates significantly more revenue per unit of duty paid.

For a US importer building an assortment in 2026, the sensible structure is to lead with the electrics for margin and use moulded drinkware for volume and repeat orders, rather than trying to compete on a container of commodity cups.

sections.h2: Two fees you can actually reduce
body: The merchandise processing fee is charged per formal entry, with a minimum and a maximum set annually, and the harbour maintenance fee applies to ocean cargo as a percentage of value. Neither is a tariff, and both are per-shipment charges rather than per-unit ones.

That makes consolidation a genuine cost lever. Three suppliers shipping to you separately means three entries and three processing fee minimums. One supplier consolidating the same goods into one shipment means one entry and one fee — and usually a better freight rate, because a full cube loads more efficiently than three partial ones. When you compare a factory-direct quote against a domestic distributor, put the fee structure next to the unit price; on mixed orders it is not a rounding error.

sections.h2: How to build a landed cost you can trust
bullets: Get the correct HTS classification in writing from a licensed broker before you commit to a retail price
Ask the supplier for material composition, intended use and whether the item contains electronics
Confirm whether the product is a set or a single article, since sets are classified differently
Add the merchandise processing fee and harbour maintenance fee as separate lines, not a percentage of goods
Ask whether the supplier can consolidate multiple categories into one shipment and one entry
Re-check the Chapter 99 position before every large order, because scope and exclusions change
body: Duty, taxes and clearance are the responsibility of the importer of record, and we are not a customs advisory service — confirm your position with your broker. What we can do is supply the documentation and product data your broker needs to classify the goods correctly, and ship consolidated so you pay one entry instead of three.

faqs.q: What is the duty rate on plastic drinkware from China?
faqs.a: The base MFN rate for plastic tableware under HTS heading 3924 is 3.4%, but Section 301 trade-action layers and an additional forced-labour action effective July 2026 are added on top in Chapter 99. The effective rate is therefore materially higher than the base rate. Confirm the current position with your customs broker before committing to a landed cost.

faqs.q: Which is cheaper to import, drinkware or kitchen electrics?
faqs.a: Per unit of value, kitchen electrics such as rechargeable grinders, frothers and wine openers sit in a materially better duty band than plastic tableware under heading 3924, and they carry much higher unit values. Many importers use electrics for margin and moulded drinkware for volume.

faqs.q: Can you reduce my fees?
faqs.a: We cannot change duty rates, but consolidating multiple categories into one shipment means one customs entry instead of several, which reduces per-shipment processing fees and usually improves the freight rate.

faqs.q: Do you provide documentation for customs?
faqs.a: Yes. We supply material composition, intended use, carton and weight data, and material certificates so your broker can classify the goods correctly. Duty and clearance remain the importer's responsibility.

faqs.q: What product data do you provide for customs classification?
faqs.a: We provide the model, the material, the capacity, the unit weight, the case pack and the carton dimensions per SKU, which is the data a broker needs to classify the goods. Import duty, taxes and clearance are the responsibility of the importer of record.

faqs.q: Do the delivery terms change the duty position?
faqs.a: The delivery term changes who arranges and pays the freight and the clearance, not the duty rate that applies to the goods. Confirm the term you want in the quotation request so the pricing basis is stated clearly.

faqs.q: Can electrical products and drinkware ship together?
faqs.a: They are quoted together and consolidated for shipment, but they are classified separately, so the classification data is provided per SKU rather than per shipment.

title: Champagne flutes vs coupes: choosing the right glass for an event
h1: Champagne flutes vs coupes: choosing the right glass for an event
author: BYF BOOM Events Team
excerpt: The flute keeps the bubbles and the coupe keeps the photograph. Which one belongs on your table depends on the service, the venue and the budget line.
seoTitle: Champagne Flutes vs Coupes: Which Glass for Your Event?
seoDescription: Compare champagne flutes and coupes for events: bubble retention, pouring practicalities, photography, breakage risk in service and wholesale cost per piece.

sections.h2: What each shape does well
body: A flute is a engineering solution to a physics problem: the narrow bowl reduces surface area, so dissolved carbon dioxide escapes more slowly and the bubbles last through a long toast. A coupe trades that bubble retention for a wide, shallow bowl that presents the drink and photographs beautifully, and it is far easier to serve from — a coupe does not overflow when a server is pouring for eighty people at speed.

The third option, and the one event buyers increasingly specify, is the stemless flute. It removes the stem joint that fails first when glasses are packed, stacked and unpacked, which in a moulded glass means the whole piece is one continuous form.

sections.h2: The service practicalities nobody mentions
bullets: Flutes pour slowly and need a steadier hand; a coupe tolerates a faster pour
Coupes spill more readily from a tray on an uneven floor
Stemless shapes stack more efficiently in storage than stemmed ones
Ribbed or textured walls hide fingerprints, which matters on a photographed table
Square profiles pack denser per carton, which lowers freight cost per piece
body: If your service is a standing reception with trays moving through a crowd, flutes and stemless flutes are the safer choice. If it is a seated dinner where glasses go onto a table and stay there, a coupe looks better and is easier to pour.

sections.h2: Choosing by venue
body: Indoors with staff and a steady floor, either shape works. Outdoors, on gravel, on a terrace or by a pool, the choice narrows: the lower the centre of gravity the better, which favours stemless and coupe shapes. For a venue with a glass ban, a ribbed coupe in PS or acrylic reads as premium crystal in low light while costing a fraction of what a glass replacement programme would.

Photography is worth thinking about explicitly, because an event's marketing depends on it. A ribbed coupe with a garnish photographs as well as anything on the table, and it does so at a lower unit cost than a stemmed crystal flute.

sections.h2: Specifying the right quantity
body: Whichever shape you pick, plan on roughly 1.2 pieces per guest for a toast-only service and 2.5 pieces per guest when the reception runs a full programme. Where the bar is outdoors, add 15% for loss instead of 10%.
Mixing shapes inside one order is fine and often better: flutes for the toast, coupes for the cocktail hour, both in the same finish so the table still reads as a set.

faqs.q: Do coupes make champagne go flat faster?
faqs.a: Yes. A coupe has more surface area than a flute, so dissolved gas escapes more quickly. For a toast that lasts a few minutes this is not noticeable; for a drink nursed over an hour the flute is better.

faqs.q: Are ribbed champagne flutes more expensive?
faqs.a: Ribbed moulds are slightly more expensive per piece than plain ones, but the difference is small compared with the perceived quality gain in photography and on the table.

faqs.q: Which is better for an outdoor event?
faqs.a: Choose a lower centre of gravity: stemless flutes or coupes. Both are more stable on uneven ground and terraces than a tall stemmed flute.

faqs.q: Can I order both shapes in the same colour?
faqs.a: Yes. Colour matching to Pantone is available across all moulded lines, so flutes and coupes can be produced in one finish as a matched set.

faqs.q: Which shape should a venue choose for a toast?
faqs.a: The flute preserves the bead and suits a standing toast; the coupe has a wider bowl and suits a seated serve or a cocktail programme. Confirm the serve and the venue so the shape matches how the drink is poured.

faqs.q: Can both shapes be ordered in the same programme?
faqs.a: Yes. Mixed shapes are quoted with the quantity per shape, and the order is consolidated into a single shipment.

faqs.q: Does the shape affect the decoration area?
faqs.a: Yes. The available decoration area follows the surface available on that shape, so the artwork treatment is confirmed for the selected SKU rather than applied across a category.

title: How to build a promotional drinkware programme that actually reorders
h1: How to build a promotional drinkware programme that actually reorders
author: BYF BOOM Distributor Team
excerpt: The difference between a one-off branded order and a programme is specification consistency. Here is how to structure an assortment that survives three seasons.
seoTitle: Building a Promotional Drinkware Programme That Reorders | BYF BOOM
seoDescription: How distributors and importers structure branded drinkware programmes so items reorder consistently: specification control, tiered pricing, packaging and decoration planning.

sections.h2: The reorder is the business
body: A single branded order is a transaction. A programme is an account that comes back every season with a list rather than a question. The difference almost always comes down to one thing: whether the item the client reordered is the same item they received the first time.

In drinkware this fails more often than buyers expect, and it fails quietly. A trading-company supplier sources from whatever factory has capacity; the second order arrives with a marginally thicker rim or a lighter base. Nobody complains formally, but the client notices, and the next year they go out to tender.

sections.h2: Structure the assortment in three tiers
bullets: A hero item — one distinctive piece that anchors the offer visually, such as an electroplated disco ball cup, a beer bat or a ribbed coupe
Two or three volume items — plain drinkware that carries the price and the quantity, ideally in a matched silhouette
Two or three small add-ons — pourers, stoppers or champagne sippers, where the low unit cost lets the client hit a gifting budget without changing the order size
body: The add-ons matter more than their revenue suggests. A branded pourer at a few thousand pieces is often the item that makes a client's per-guest giveaway budget work, and once it is in the printed programme it reorders on the same cycle as the glasses.

sections.h2: Control the specification, not just the price
body: Put the specification in writing and keep it: material, capacity, unit weight, rim profile, carton count. Those are the five things that drift between factories. When your supplier owns the tooling, the specification is a property of the mould rather than a promise in an email, which is why factory-direct sourcing is worth more on the third order than on the first.

Carton count deserves specific attention. A client's storeroom and their distributor's pallet plan are built around it. Changing it silently is the fastest way to create a logistical problem in someone else's operation.

sections.h2: Plan decoration and packaging together
body: Decoration and packaging are where programmes lose margin, because they are usually quoted last. Ask for them as separate lines on the first quotation: print method, number of colours, setup, MOQ for the decorated version, and packaging cost. If retail shelf or e-commerce is in the client's future, add the colour box, hang tag and UPC barcode at the start — retrofitting packaging to a live listing is far more expensive than planning it in.

Where the client's mark has to survive repeated washing or years of use, specify laser engraving over pad printing. It costs more per unit and it removes the complaint that the logo wore off, which is the complaint that ends programmes.

sections.h2: Make the first order survivable
body: A programme that starts with a container's worth of unproven stock rarely gets the chance to become a programme. Tiered pricing at case, pallet and container quantities lets you place a first order that proves the item, then scale the identical product once it does. Because the tooling does not change between those tiers, the item that proves out at case quantity is the item you scale — not a near-match from another supplier.

faqs.q: What makes a branded drinkware item reorder?
faqs.a: Specification consistency. If the reordered item matches the original in rim thickness, base weight and carton count, the client reorders. That is why sourcing from the factory that owns the mould matters more on the second and third order than on the first.

faqs.q: What should be in a promotional drinkware assortment?
faqs.a: A three-tier structure works best: one distinctive hero item, two or three volume drinkware items in a matched silhouette, and two or three low-cost add-ons such as pourers or stoppers that let the client hit a per-guest budget.

faqs.q: Should I use pad printing or laser engraving?
faqs.a: Use pad printing for short runs and one or two colours where unit cost is the priority. Use laser engraving where the item will be washed repeatedly or kept as a keepsake, because the mark cannot wear off.

faqs.q: Can I start with a small order and scale later?
faqs.a: Yes. The price is quoted per project for the quantity you need, and because the tooling does not change between volumes the product you scale is identical to the one you tested.

faqs.q: What records make a programme reproducible?
faqs.a: The SKU, the mould record, the material, the decoration method, the Pantone reference, the packing configuration and the approved pre-production sample. Those records are the reorder brief.

faqs.q: How far ahead should the second run be planned?
faqs.a: Plan the reorder against the production route and the destination lead time that apply to your SKUs, not against a general figure. Send the in-hands date and the SKUs and the FOB dispatch timing is confirmed for that route.

faqs.q: Can the decoration change between runs?
faqs.a: Artwork changes are treated as a new brief and are re-approved, because the decoration method, the area and the proof all have to match the new artwork before production starts.

title: Logo Decoration on Barware and Drinkware: Artwork, Position and Approval
h1: How logo decoration on barware and drinkware is specified
author: BYF BOOM Product Team
excerpt: What to send, what decides feasibility, and what has to be approved before a branded run starts — without assuming one method fits every material.
seoTitle: Logo Decoration on Barware and Drinkware | BYF BOOM
seoDescription: How logo decoration is specified for wholesale barware and drinkware: artwork files, decoration area, colour count, method selection and pre-production approval.
keywords: pad printing vs laser engraving drinkware

sections.h2: Start from the artwork, not from the method
body: The single biggest cause of a late branded order is artwork that cannot be produced as supplied. Send the logo as vector artwork — AI, EPS or PDF with the text converted to outlines — and state the Pantone reference for each colour. That gives a decoration area that can be measured and a colour that can be matched, instead of a screenshot that has to be redrawn.

If only a raster file exists, we confirm whether it can be reproduced cleanly at the size the item allows. A redraw is a separate step and belongs in the schedule, not in the week the goods were supposed to ship.

sections.h2: Decoration area and colour count decide feasibility
body: The available decoration area follows the surface of the selected item. A tall flute and a short shot glass offer very different usable areas, and a curved surface reduces the area that will reproduce cleanly compared with a flat panel. This is why we confirm feasibility against the exact SKU rather than approving a logo across a whole range.

Colour count changes both cost and feasibility. Each additional colour on a printed mark adds a setup and a pass, and on a moulded or coated surface the substrate has to accept the ink reliably. Where a client wants four colours on a small curved area, the honest answer is often that the artwork needs simplifying for that item.

sections.h2: Choosing between a printed mark and a permanent mark
body: A printed mark is the lower-cost route and suits short runs, multi-colour artwork and flat or gently curved areas. An engraved mark is cut into the material rather than sitting on the surface, which matters for items that will be washed repeatedly or kept as a keepsake — the mark cannot wear off because it is not a layer.

Which methods are actually available depends on the material and the shape, so they are confirmed for the SKU you select. Engraving is not appropriate on every surface, and printing is not appropriate where the mark has to survive years of washing.

sections.h2: What has to be approved before production starts
body: The production brief is what the run is judged against, so it is approved as a whole: the SKU specification, the artwork, the logo position, the decoration method, the packaging build, the quantity and the destination.

Where the appearance is colour sensitive, a colour chip or a pre-production sample is approved before the bulk run. That step exists to protect both sides: it is far cheaper to reject a sample than to reject a container.

sections.h2: Care after decoration
body: The care instruction for a decorated item follows the material of the item. Warm soapy water and a soft cloth are appropriate for a printed mark; abrasive scouring pads and very hot cycles are not, because they attack the ink film rather than the item.
Where an item is expected to be washed by housekeeping or by a venue's glasswash operation every day, that is a reason to specify a permanent mark rather than a cheaper printed one.

faqs.q: What artwork file should I provide for a logo on drinkware or barware?
faqs.a: Vector artwork — AI, EPS or PDF with the text converted to outlines — plus the Pantone reference for each colour. If only a raster file exists, we confirm whether it reproduces cleanly at the size the selected item allows, and any redraw is scheduled as a separate step.

faqs.q: How do logo position and colour count affect decoration feasibility?
faqs.a: The available decoration area follows the surface of the selected SKU, and a curved surface reduces the area that prints cleanly compared with a flat panel. Each additional colour adds a setup and a pass, so colour count affects both cost and feasibility and is confirmed for the exact item.

faqs.q: When is laser engraving suitable, and when is printing the better route?
faqs.a: Engraving suits items that will be washed repeatedly or kept as a keepsake, because the mark is cut into the material rather than sitting on the surface. Printing suits short runs and multi-colour artwork where unit cost is the priority. Which methods apply is confirmed for the SKU and material you select.

faqs.q: What must be approved before branded production starts?
faqs.a: The SKU specification, the artwork, the logo position, the decoration method, the packaging build, the quantity and the final production brief. Where the appearance is colour sensitive, a colour chip or a pre-production sample is approved before the bulk run.

faqs.q: How should branded drinkware be cared for after decoration?
faqs.a: Follow the care instruction for the material of the item: warm soapy water and a soft cloth. Abrasive scouring pads and very hot cycles are not appropriate for a printed mark because they attack the ink film. Where an item is washed daily, specify a permanent mark.

faqs.q: Can you match a specific Pantone reference for the logo?
faqs.a: Colour is matched to the Pantone reference you supply, and where the appearance is colour sensitive a colour chip or pre-production sample is approved before the bulk run. The match is confirmed against the substrate of the selected SKU, because the same ink reads differently on a moulded surface and a coated one.

faqs.q: What happens if the artwork changes after it has been approved?
faqs.a: A change to approved artwork is treated as a new brief. The artwork, the decoration area and the proof are re-approved before production resumes, and a change to the method or the area is re-quoted.

title: Gift Box Packaging for Barware and Drinkware Sets
h1: How a barware gift-box build is specified
author: BYF BOOM Product Team
excerpt: A gift set is a build rather than a product: contents, insert, box, branding and outer carton are confirmed together, and the minimum belongs to the build.
seoTitle: Gift Box Packaging for Barware Sets | BYF BOOM
seoDescription: How gift-box packaging is specified for wholesale barware and drinkware sets: contents, insert, branding, box format, export protection and the build minimum.

sections.h2: A gift set is a build, not a product
body: The mistake in gift-set sourcing is quoting item by item and assuming the box is packaging. A set is one build: the items, the insert, the gift box, the logo treatment, the outer carton and the quantity are confirmed together, because a change to any one of them changes the others.

That is also why the minimum for a gift set is not the minimum of the item inside it. The build is a different production route with its own setup, so the confirmed figure is issued for the build rather than inferred from the bulk minimum.

sections.h2: The insert decides whether the set arrives intact
body: The insert is the part that protects the product and the part that customers never see until they open the box — and it is usually where a set fails. Cavity shape, material, thickness and tolerance all determine whether the item sits still in transit or arrives with the decoration rubbed.
Confirm the insert together with the item list. A last-minute change to contents is not a small change: it re-cuts the insert and can change the box size and the outer carton count with it.

sections.h2: Branding the box itself
body: Branding on a box is a different exercise from decorating the item. Board material, print method, colour count and finish all affect how the artwork reads, and a logo that works on a moulded surface may need adjusting for a printed board surface.
Send the artwork and the intended box format together so the box branding and the item decoration are approved as one visual result rather than two independent jobs.

sections.h2: Export packing around a retail box
body: A retail or gift box is not the shipping carton unless it is specified as one. The outer carton, the protection around the box and the carton count are confirmed as part of the build so the set survives the route it actually travels.

State the destination and whether the goods will be handled by a distributor or a fulfilment centre before they are sold. The number of handling steps is what determines how much protection the outer carton needs.

sections.h2: Plan the set list early
body: The contents decide the insert, the insert decides the box, and the box decides the outer carton. Every one of those steps has a lead time attached, so the set list is the first thing to fix and the last thing to change.
If the composition is still open when artwork is ready, send the options rather than picking one silently. We will confirm which options share an insert and which ones need their own.

faqs.q: What has to be specified for a gift-box build?
faqs.a: The contents and quantities, the insert, the gift box, the logo treatment on both the item and the box, the outer carton and the total build quantity. They are confirmed together because a change to any one of them changes the others.

faqs.q: Does a gift-box build change the minimum order?
faqs.a: Yes, potentially. A gift-box build is a different production route from the blank bulk order for the same item, so it carries its own confirmed minimum rather than the bulk minimum. The figure is issued with the quotation for the build.

faqs.q: How is a gift set protected for export?
faqs.a: The insert holds the item, the box presents it, and the outer carton protects the box for the route it travels. Protection is specified against the destination and the number of handling steps, and the carton count is stated so freight can be planned.

faqs.q: Can the gift box itself be branded?
faqs.a: Yes, subject to confirmation of the board material, the print method, the colour count and the quantity. Send the artwork and the intended box format together so the box and the item are approved as one visual result.

faqs.q: Can I mix items from different categories in one box?
faqs.a: Yes. Send the complete item list with the quantity per item, the insert requirement and the packaging configuration. A mixed-category set is quoted as one build and consolidated into a single shipment.

faqs.q: Can I supply my own box design?
faqs.a: Yes. Send the box artwork, the format and the material specification you want and we confirm it against the items that go inside. Where the format is fixed by your design, the insert is built to fit it rather than the box being changed to fit the insert.

faqs.q: What information should appear on the box or the insert for retail?
faqs.a: Confirm what the end customer needs to read: the item description, the care instruction and any barcode or marking required by your sales channel. That content is printed on the insert or the box and is approved together with the rest of the artwork.

title: How model, colour and packaging set your MOQ
h1: How model, colour and packaging set your minimum order
author: BYF BOOM Product Team
excerpt: Why one total quantity is never the whole answer: how the model, colour split, logo versions, accessories, printed packaging and the mould decision each set the workable minimum — and how to plan a first order that stays simple.
seoTitle: How Model, Colour and Packaging Set Your MOQ | BYF BOOM
seoDescription: How model choice, colour splits, logo versions, accessories, printed packaging and new moulds change the workable minimum order.

sections.h2: A minimum is the smallest complete production plan, not a number
body: When a buyer asks for a minimum order quantity, the useful answer is not the smallest number we can type. It is the smallest order that can be run as one controlled plan: materials sourced, moulds allocated, decoration set up, components counted, packaging printed and goods inspected — all against a written specification.

One total quantity can hide many smaller batches. The same order split across several capacities, several colours and two logo versions is not one production group; it is several, and each has to be identified, decorated, counted and packed correctly. That is why we do not publish a category-wide figure on this site: it would describe an order that nobody actually places.

The product is only one layer. A printed box runs in its own economic quantities. A lid, an insert or an LED module is a separate supply line. A new colour needs approval and process control. A new mould is a development project that happens before any bulk output. Send the full breakdown and we can tell you which part of your project sets the practical minimum.

sections.h2: Route one: an existing model with limited variation
body: The most practical first order usually starts from a model that already exists. You pick a current body — a wine glass, a stopper, an ice bucket — and keep the first project to a clear specification: one or two colours, one logo file, one packaging format.

Every product page in our catalogue records the capacity, case pack, material and carton data for that model, so the discussion starts from a real body rather than a photograph. Existing models remove most of the product-development work, but they do not remove the need to confirm decoration and packaging; they simply give both sides something real to sample and measure.

sections.h2: Route two: decoration and accessories create their own minimums
body: A plain product and a finished private-label item are not the same order. Logo printing, colour coating or engraving each carry setup work and an approved sample. Several artwork versions divide the run into smaller groups. A lid, a sleeve, an insert or an LED module adds another supply line, and if the accessory colour changes, the order divides again.
These are the questions that decide it:
bullets: How many body models and capacities are involved?
How many colours, and how many pieces per colour?
How many logo files or logo colours, and what quantity per version?
Which accessories belong to each selling unit?
Does every item use the same pack structure?
Is it one shipment, or several destination-specific lots?

sections.h2: Route three: a new mould changes the conversation
body: We are a mould factory — the tooling is ours, and we run roughly two hundred new items a year. So when a buyer wants a shape that does not exist in the catalogue, the conversation is not about minimums at all; it is about a development project. Drawing review, tooling, trials and sample approval happen before any bulk production, and the economics of the order have to support that work.

A new mould makes sense when the shape creates real value: a protected brand silhouette, a functional improvement, a required dimension, or a collection you intend to reorder. If a current model meets the use and most of the visual goal, we will show you that route first — we would rather earn the reorder than sell the tooling.

When a supplier quotes a new shape at the same minimum and lead time as a catalogue item, check what is actually being promised. An existing model with decoration and a newly moulded body may share a product name, but they are not equivalent production plans.

sections.h2: Printed packaging is the hidden minimum
body: Packaging is usually the last detail a buyer sends and the first reason a small project becomes expensive. A plain export carton, a custom colour box and a rigid gift set are different materials, different setup and different run quantities. Inserts have to fit spouts, lids and accessories. Several language or barcode versions divide the packaging run even when the product is identical.

For a trial order we often recommend a standard protective structure with a simpler label or sleeve, then move to fully printed boxes once the assortment proves itself. The right answer depends on the channel: a retail buyer needs shelf information, an e-commerce seller needs parcel protection, and a venue buyer needs safe bulk handling more than a presentation box.

sections.h2: How we simplify a first order
body: A low-risk trial order is not a big assortment made small. It is a focused assortment designed to answer one commercial question. If the goal is to test demand, we usually recommend one existing shape, one or two capacities, fewer colours, one logo file and one packaging route. The first order then tells you which colour or capacity deserves the reorder.

We also keep sample quantity and bulk quantity separate. A sample exists to approve a product, a decoration or a pack; it does not prove that the same unit price applies to a small bulk run. Samples and bulk production are planned differently, and quoting them as if they were the same thing is how buyers end up comparing numbers that describe different orders.

sections.h2: Why a very small minimum inflates the unit price
body: Some setup work exists whether the order is large or small: artwork checking, decoration setup, packaging development, carton marks, sample approval and inspection planning. Spread that fixed work over fewer finished units and the unit price rises — that is arithmetic, not policy.

Freight distorts the comparison further. Drinkware is light but voluminous, so a small shipment still needs full protective cartons. Compare the total landed project — product, decoration, packaging, freight and destination charges — not the unit price alone. We would rather show you two clear routes, a simple one and a fully customised one, than quote a number that hides the difference.

sections.h2: Quality control does not become optional because the order is small
body: A trial order still needs a defined approval standard. We check goods against the confirmed model and the approved sample: capacity and dimensions where relevant, rim and finish, decoration, set count and carton protection. Small orders are more sensitive to error, not less, because there are fewer spare units and more variant splits to count. If four colours are packed into one set, counting accuracy is the difference between a saleable set and a return.

sections.h2: What to send before we can confirm a minimum
body: Send a short, specific brief and we will tell you which part of the project controls the minimum — and which change would make the first order easier to produce and repeat:
bullets: Product link, model number, drawing or reference photo
Target material and capacity
Total order quantity
Quantity per size, colour and logo version
Accessories or set components per selling unit
Retail, gift, e-commerce or bulk pack requirement
Destination country or warehouse
Target dispatch or launch date

faqs.q: Why don't you publish a minimum order quantity on each product page?
faqs.a: Because a single figure would describe an order nobody places. The workable minimum depends on the selected model, the colour split, the logo versions, the accessories and the packaging — all of which are configurable. We confirm it per project, in writing, against your full breakdown.

faqs.q: Does a custom colour change the minimum?
faqs.a: It can. What matters is the quantity per colour, not just the total. One colour across the whole order is one production group; four colours divide the run into four groups that each need process control, counting and packing.

faqs.q: Does adding a logo change the minimum?
faqs.a: Often yes. Each decoration process carries setup work and an approved first-off. One logo in one colour is a single group; several artwork versions or several logo colours divide the run again.

faqs.q: Does the packaging have its own minimum?
faqs.a: It can. Printed boxes, inserts and labels run in their own economic quantities, and language or barcode versions divide the run. We review product and packaging together so the minimum you receive describes the finished item, not the bare product.

faqs.q: Is the sample minimum the same as the bulk minimum?
faqs.a: No. A sample exists to approve a product, a decoration or a pack; it is planned and priced differently from bulk production. A sample proves the specification — it does not set the price of a small bulk run.

faqs.q: Can we start with a small test order?
faqs.a: Send your real target quantity and we will review it honestly. An existing model with limited customisation is the most realistic route, and we cannot promise that every project runs below its planning minimum. Simplifying capacities, colours, logos and printed packaging usually does more than negotiating the number.

faqs.q: How do we bring the minimum down?
faqs.a: Start from an existing model, hold one or two capacities, reduce the colour count, use one logo file and one pack structure. That keeps the order in the fewest production groups, and the first order then tells you which variant deserves the reorder.

faqs.q: Does a new mould raise the minimum?
faqs.a: A new mould is a development project — drawing review, tooling, trials and sample approval — priced separately from bulk production. The mould does not so much raise the minimum as change what the order has to support: it makes sense when the shape creates real value and you intend to reorder.

faqs.q: Another supplier quoted a lower minimum. Why?
faqs.a: Check what the two numbers describe. One may cover a plain product in bulk packing; the other a logo, a colour box and several colours. Compare the total landed project — product, decoration, packaging, freight and destination charges — and the specification each price is issued against.

title: How to prepare a drinkware RFQ that returns a firm price
h1: How to prepare a drinkware RFQ that returns a firm price
author: BYF BOOM Product Team
excerpt: The most useful first enquiry makes the finished product visible: model, capacity, quantity split, logo, packaging, destination and date. Here is the checklist we work from — and a plain-text template you can copy.
seoTitle: How to Prepare a Drinkware RFQ That Returns a Firm Price
seoDescription: A supply-side RFQ checklist for wholesale drinkware: model, capacity, quantity split, logo, packaging, destination and samples — with a copy-paste template.

sections.h2: A good RFQ is short, but it makes the product visible
body: The hardest enquiries to answer are not the short ones — they are the ones that leave out the quantity per size, the accessories in one selling unit, or the destination. When those details are missing, the supplier fills the gaps with assumptions, and the prices that come back look comparable but describe different products.

A good RFQ identifies the product, the capacity, the quantity and its split, the customisation, the packaging, the destination and the date. If a decision is still open, say so — an open question gets one clarifying reply; a wrong assumption gets a quotation for the wrong product.

sections.h2: Start from the closest model
body: Send a product link, a model number, a drawing or a reference photo. A model number is best because it connects your enquiry to a real body — the capacity, the material and the case pack already exist on the record.

If your reference comes from another source, say which features must match and which can change. Do not assume a photograph carries dimensions: perspective distorts proportions, and most product images never show the usable capacity.

sections.h2: State the use and the sales channel
body: A tasting-room merchandise glass, a six-piece retail set, a banquet tumbler and an e-commerce gift item need different accessories, decoration and packing. The channel also decides which use statements matter. We do not infer washing, microwave or thermal performance from appearance — if your market needs a specific claim, name it so it can be reviewed against the selected product and the evidence on file.

sections.h2: Give the capacity and the dimensions that must fit
body: Capacity affects the body, the pack size and the freight volume. Write the target in millilitres or ounces and say whether it is fixed. If a dimension matters — a refrigerator door, a shelf height, an existing lid — include it, and for sets list the capacity of every component. When several sizes are involved, list the quantity for each: a capacity range is not one product.

sections.h2: Show the total quantity and the complete split
body: A total on its own is not enough once the order contains several colours, capacities or logos. Write the total, then break it down — quantity per size, per colour, per logo version, and how the pieces pack into sets. The same total divided differently is a different production plan, and it is the split, not the headline, that sets the workable minimum.

sections.h2: Define the logo and the visible customisation
body: Attach a vector file if you have one, and state the colour, the approximate size, the position and the process if you know it. If you do not know the process, describe the appearance and the use condition and we will propose one. For colour projects, give a controlled reference such as a Pantone number and the quantity per colour.

Treat the product artwork and the packaging artwork as two separate files and two separate approvals. A clear artwork file reduces sampling errors, and the approved decorated sample is what controls bulk production.

sections.h2: List every component in one selling unit
body: A lid, a sleeve, a stopper, a base or an insert changes the product. Write the exact quantity of each component per unit or per set, and list replacement components separately. A quotation should state what is included, so you are never comparing a bare-product price against a complete-item price.

sections.h2: Describe the packaging and the sales unit
body: Tell us how you will receive and sell the product:
bullets: Bulk divided export carton
Individual plain or custom colour box
Pair or multi-piece retail set
Gift box with insert
E-commerce pack for single-unit delivery
Hospitality pack with practical dividers
bodyAfterBullets: State the pieces per set and any barcode, label, country-mark or carton-mark requirement. Packaging is developed around the approved product and its accessories; it affects the finished unit cost, the carton dimensions, the freight volume and the schedule. A retail box does not automatically survive last-mile parcel delivery.

sections.h2: Add the destination, the trade basis and the date that matters
body: At minimum we need the destination country or warehouse city. State the trade basis you use — FOB, EXW, DDP — or say you are unsure and we will propose a route. Freight-related prices are time-sensitive, so the destination and the quotation date matter.

Give the date the goods are needed and say what it is: a shipment date, a warehouse arrival date and a retail launch date are three different milestones, and we plan backwards from the right one. For seasonal projects, put the non-negotiable launch date in the first message — late packaging artwork is the most common way a simple order loses time.

sections.h2: Say what the sample must prove
body: A plain sample checks size and hand feel. A decorated sample approves the logo. A complete set checks component fit. A packaging sample approves the box and the insert. Say which one you need, and record the approved version — model, capacity, decoration file, accessories and pack — so production instructions never rely on scattered messages.

sections.h2: Copy this RFQ template
body: Send this in an email or through the quote form on this site. You do not need to complete every line before contacting us — mark open decisions as open.
bullets: Product or model number:
Intended use and sales channel:
Capacity and critical dimensions:
Total quantity:
Quantity per size, colour and logo version:
Logo file, colour, size and position:
Accessories or components per selling unit:
Packaging: retail, gift, e-commerce or bulk:
Destination port or city:
Trade basis (FOB / EXW / DDP):
Target date, and what that date is:
What the sample must prove:
QC or compliance requirements:

faqs.q: What is the minimum information you need for a firm quotation?
faqs.a: The closest model or reference, the capacity, the total quantity with its split per size, colour and logo version, the packaging requirement, the destination and the target date. Those details let us price the finished item rather than a bare product.

faqs.q: Can I request a quote from a photo alone?
faqs.a: Yes, as a starting point. Add the target capacity, the expected quantity, the use, the packaging and the destination, and we will compare the photo with current models and name the missing specifications before pricing.

faqs.q: Do I need finished artwork before asking for a price?
faqs.a: No. State the box type, the pieces per set, the channel and the destination. Artwork can follow — but the packaging scope has to be in the estimate, because it affects both cost and schedule.

faqs.q: Should I ask for FOB or DDP pricing?
faqs.a: State the trade basis you normally use. If you are unsure, give the destination and we will propose the available routes. Freight-related prices change over time, so they are always tied to a date.

faqs.q: What file format should the logo be?
faqs.a: A vector file is preferred when available. Also state the logo colour, the approximate size and the position. The approved decorated sample — not the file alone — is what controls bulk production.

faqs.q: How quickly can I get a sample?
faqs.a: It depends on stock status. In-stock samples are dispatched within 1–3 working days after payment is received; for no-stock small batches, including samples, FOB dispatch normally takes 10–15 days. These are dispatch times, not arrival times — destination freight is quoted separately.

faqs.q: Why do you ask for the quantity per colour?
faqs.a: Because the split, not the total, sets the production plan. Quantity per colour and per logo version decides how many production groups the order contains, which drives setup, counting, packing and cost.

faqs.q: What if I cannot answer every field?
faqs.a: Mark it as open and send the enquiry anyway. An open question gets one clarifying reply; a wrong assumption gets a quotation for the wrong product, and that costs both sides more time.
